title: What Is the Influence of Task Order in Continual Learning? An Empirical Study and Order-Aware Evaluation for Motion Forecasting

paper.title: What Is the Influence of Task Order in Continual Learning? An Empirical Study and Order-Aware Evaluation for Motion Forecasting
paper.abstract: Abstract Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90% to 99% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available here .

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Self-driving vehicles plan their motion around forecasts of where surrounding road users will go. A forecaster trained on urban merges meets highway ramps, intersections, and roundabouts as the fleet expands, and must keep learning in an order no designer controls. Continual learning (CL) provides this capability and is moving into safety-relevant applications. Human-guided CL already uses small amounts of driving guidance to improve self-driving performance in dimensions such as social compliance and rare-case handling [ 1 ] , and continual forecasting methods adapt motion predictors across changing traffic scenarios [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Learning a new task can overwrite earlier knowledge [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Replay, regularisation, and gradient constraints counter this forgetting through different retention mechanisms [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] , so their outcomes depend on the learning history fixed by the task order. Yet the algorithm to deploy is chosen from benchmark rankings. If a ranking reverses when the same tasks arrive in another sequence, that choice hinges on an arbitrary benchmark order. Because outcomes depend on the order in which tasks arrive, any aggregate score for a CL algorithm rests on a distribution over task orders. Evaluating continual forecasting under varying data-stream sequences has been recommended [ 15 ] , yet many protocols leave this distribution implicit, repeating one or a few prescribed orders while varying initialisation or within-task sample order [ 14 , 5 ] . Studies of order-dependent forgetting, order-wise performance disparity, ordering principles, and sequence transferability show that task transitions influence retention and transfer [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] , and use this to explain the outcomes of particular orders, quantify the disparity among them, or select favourable ones. How the variation of a metric across all N ! N! orders of N N tasks, several algorithms, and repeated training runs divides between order, algorithm, their interaction, and training randomness, and which property of an order carries the order effect, remain open. This paper answers both questions for a fixed task set and tests whether algorithm rankings persist across orders. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over an explicit order policy, with the uniform policy as the equal-order reference, and decompose the sum of squares of each metric into order, algorithm, interaction, and training components, splitting the order term by starting task. A replicate bootstrap attaches a probability to every leading algorithm. A warm-start current-task error and a decomposition of backward transfer into subsequent error and initial reference isolate the first learning stage. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics defines a descriptor-weighted policy, an example of a nonuniform policy shared by all algorithms (Figs. 1 (b) and 2 ). The experiments use the UQnet endpoint-heatmap backbone [ 20 ] and four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset: Urban Merge (A), Highway Merge (B), Intersection (C), and Roundabout (D). Vanilla sequential fine-tuning and three memory-based algorithms learn the tasks in all 4 ! = 24 4!=24 orders, with three training replicates per order and algorithm (288 runs). The memory-based algorithms are dark experience replay (DER), synergetic memory rehearsal (SyReM), and gradient scenario memory (GSM). In Fig. 1 (a), A → \to B → \to C → \to D and A → \to B → \to D → \to C differ only in their final two tasks, yet give exactly reversed rankings of the four algorithms by current-task final displacement error. Section VI-A traces both rankings to run-to-run variation in the cold-start error, which arises on the shared first task before the two orders diverge. The main contributions are summarised as follows. 1. Formulation and benchmark. An expectation over an explicit order policy defines a common comparison target, and the law of total variance separates within-order training variation from across-order variation. All 24 orders are enumerated with released per-run results, and the decomposition, adjustment, and bootstrap procedures form a reusable analysis toolkit. 2. Empirical finding. Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90% to 99% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task, acting through the cold start of the smallest task. Beyond the first stage, the residual order effect is comparable to training variability. The per-order leader’s gap to the runner-up exceeds the pooled replicate standard deviation in only 2 to 11 of the 24 orders for current-task error and backward transfer, against 16 or 17 for final error. 3. Metric diagnosis. The first task enters the reference term of stage-averaged backward transfer with weight 11 / 18 11/18 for four tasks, so a poor first fit simultaneously raises current-task error and drives backward transfer towards large negative values. Relative improvement and absolute final error therefore identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. The transition-direction descriptor tracks the position of the smallest task, and the descriptor-weighted policy leaves the full ranking unchanged. Fig. 2: Order-aware evaluation workflow. (1) Tasks differ in size and speed distribution. (2) Each algorithm learns every order, starting cold in the first stage. (3) Testing all tasks after each stage gives the stage–task errors R r , i R_{r,i} , summarised by CT, CT 2 : N \mathrm{CT}_{2:N} , BWT = P − B \mathrm{BWT}=P-B , and the final error. (4) W1 speed distances between consecutive tasks, Δ r \Delta_{r} , define the descriptor D ⁡ ( o ) D(o) . (5) A common order policy q ⁡ ( o ) q(o) yields policy scores, and a sum-of-squares decomposition (FDE-CT) and a replicate bootstrap assess them. Networks, policy weights, and comparison marks are schematic.

sections.heading: II-A Task Order and Curriculum Effects
sections.text: Curriculum learning investigates the effect of example or task presentation on optimisation [ 21 ] . In CL, ordering also affects retention of previous knowledge. Bell and Lawrence [ 16 ] examine order-dependent forgetting and task-distance heuristics, and Li and Hiratani [ 18 ] derive ordering principles in a teacher–student model. Analyses of task similarity and overparameterisation further characterise interference [ 22 ] . Nguyen et al. [ 23 ] relate error rates to the total complexity of a task sequence and to its sequential heterogeneity, the sum of distances between consecutive tasks. The path length L L in Section IV-D is such a sum. Yoon et al. [ 17 ] quantify order-wise performance disparity, establishing order fairness as an evaluation criterion. Measures of sequence transferability relate task transitions to performance using learned predictors [ 19 ] . The present analysis uses marginal task statistics to define a shared order policy and asks how much of an observed ranking survives a change of order.

sections.heading: II-B Continual Learning for Motion Forecasting
sections.text: Continual forecasting addresses adaptation across changing traffic environments [ 15 ] through generative replay [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] , regularisation under distribution shift [ 27 ] , and task-free streams without supplied task boundaries [ 2 , 5 , 28 ] . D-GSM uses traffic divergence and scenario-organised memory to constrain gradient updates [ 3 ] , H2C combines diversity-based selection with equiprobable replay [ 5 ] , SyReM integrates a memory-loss constraint with gradient-based rehearsal selection [ 4 ] , and Dual-LS coordinates long- and short-term knowledge through complementary rehearsal [ 6 ] . These studies evaluate each method along one or a few task orders, so the dependence of the resulting ranking on the order is still unexamined.

sections.heading: II-C Evaluation Protocols for Continual Learning
sections.text: Average performance over all tasks, current-task performance, and backward transfer are the standard quantities of continual learning evaluation [ 12 , 29 ] , and the appropriate protocol differs between task-, domain-, and class-incremental settings [ 30 ] . Early protocol studies showed that reported forgetting depends on the evaluation design, including the task sequences used [ 31 , 32 ] , and proposed metric sets beyond final accuracy [ 33 ] . Hyperparameter selection on the evaluation scenario can bias comparisons [ 34 ] , and unequal update costs can alter conclusions about online CL [ 35 ] . Recent benchmarks treat the order either as an adversarial choice to be searched [ 36 ] or as a sampled factor whose uncertainty is reported [ 37 ] . Order coverage is therefore a protocol choice. We distinguish repeated training within an order from evaluation across orders, separate the starting task from the remaining order, and assess backward transfer alongside initial, warm-start, and final error.

sections.heading: IV-A Distances Between Task Distributions
sections.text: We describe each task through empirical distributions of target-agent speed and acceleration. Speed is the norm of the two velocity components at each of nine historical time steps, and acceleration is the adjacent speed difference divided by 0.1 s, retaining values in [ − 5 , 5 ] [-5,5] m/s 2 . Observations are pooled over time steps and trajectories within each task. The candidate measures probe complementary aspects of distribution shift. Wasserstein-1 (W1) quantifies displacement of probability mass along the physical feature axis [ 38 ] . Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence measures directed probability mismatch, whereas Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence provides a symmetric, bounded comparison of the same histograms [ 39 ] . Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) compares kernel mean embeddings without histogram discretisation [ 40 ] . Applying all four measures to speed holds the feature representation fixed while varying the notion of discrepancy, whereas applying W1 additionally to acceleration examines a different aspect of motion with the same distance functional. For feature f ∈ { speed , acceleration } f\in\{\text{speed},\text{acceleration}\} , let F i f F_{i}^{f} denote its empirical cumulative distribution function in task i i . We compute d i ​ j W ​ ( f ) = ∫ ℝ | F i f ​ ( t ) − F j f ​ ( t ) | ​ 𝑑 t , d^{\rm W}_{ij}(f)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F_{i}^{f}(t)-F_{j}^{f}(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t, (8) using every retained observation. The distance is expressed in m/s for speed and m/s 2 for acceleration. KL and JS divergences are computed on H = 100 H=100 shared equal-width speed histograms with additive smoothing, and MMD on a fixed standardised sample of 2,000 2{,}000 speed observations per task with a Gaussian kernel (Appendix A-A ). W1, JS, and MMD are symmetric, whereas KL is directed. The primary distance is W1 on speed, which has an interpretable physical scale. It was chosen in an exploratory scan of 20 distance representations and 15 aggregation operators against the CL outcomes (Appendix A-B ), from which the five candidates above are reported.

sections.heading: IV-D Analysis Protocol
sections.text: The decomposition and the bootstrap operate on individual runs, and the other analyses use the replicate means y m ​ ( o , a ) y_{m}(o,a) . Decomposition. For each metric, the total centred sum of squares over all runs is split into order, algorithm, order–algorithm interaction, and within-cell training components (Appendix A-C ). The order component is further split into starting-task identity and order within starting task, and the decomposition is repeated for the 18 orders that do not start with task A. Warm-start error. To separate the first stage, which involves no previous task, from the continual part of a run, the current-task error is also reported without its first term (Section V-C ). Associations. Spearman correlations with the 16 algorithm–metric series use average ranks for ties. Starting-task dependence is assessed by excluding A-first orders and by correlating ranked variables after removing starting-task group means. The same residualisation with position-of-A group means isolates what D D adds beyond the position of task A. Replicate bootstrap. The three replicates of every order–algorithm cell are resampled with replacement (5,000 draws, fixed seed), and the order means, policy scores, and per-order leaders are recomputed. This yields the probability that each algorithm attains the smallest policy score and an interval for its number of per-order wins. A per-order leader is called separable when its gap to the runner-up exceeds the pooled sample standard deviation of the two algorithms. Because the 24 orders form the complete order set, order sampling adds no uncertainty, and the resampling reflects training variation alone (Appendix A-C ). Paths. We also compare the orders with the largest and smallest total transition distance, L ⁡ ( o ) = ∑ r = 1 N − 1 d o r , o r + 1 , L(o)=\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}d_{o_{r},o_{r+1}}, (15) within each fixed starting task. Path length and slope are different summaries: L L uses all three transitions, whereas D D omits the middle one.

sections.heading: V-A Motion Forecasting Tasks and Backbone
sections.text: Each forecasting task comprises trajectory records from one category of road layout in INTERACTION [ 41 ] . Twelve location subsets are grouped into four tasks. Task A, Urban Merge , covers lane convergence and zipper merging at the German MT site. Task B, Highway Merge , covers ramp entry and lane convergence at the Chinese ZS highway site (archived subsets ZS0 and ZS2). Task C, Intersection , covers crossing and turning interactions at the US subsets MA, GL, EP0, and EP1. Task D, Roundabout , covers entry, circulation, and exit at EP, SR, and FT in the US, OF in Germany, and LN in China. The task arrays contain 5,378, 50,905, 134,269, and 103,540 trajectory records, so task A is 10 to 25 times smaller than the others. Fig. 3 compares the locations and spreads of the empirical target-agent feature distributions. Urban merging has the highest median speed (6.29 m/s), whereas highway merging combines a lower median (2.87 m/s), reflecting queuing on the ramp, with the largest 95th percentile (17.56 m/s). Intersections have the lowest median speed (2.27 m/s), and intersections and roundabouts have the wider acceleration interquartile ranges. Fig. 3: Task feature distributions. Dots, bands, and whiskers indicate medians, interquartile ranges, and 5th–95th percentiles. Acceleration is restricted to [ − 5 , 5 ] [-5,5] m/s 2 . The forecasting input is 𝐗 = ( 𝐗 TA , 𝐗 SA , 𝐌 ) \mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}_{\rm TA},\mathbf{X}_{\rm SA},\mathbf{M}) , containing the target-agent history, surrounding-agent histories, and map context. The ground-truth output 𝐘 ∈ ℝ 2 \mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} is the target endpoint. UQnet [ 20 ] combines agent and map encoders with a spatial prediction head to produce a heatmap over future endpoints, from which the predictor samples W W candidate endpoints { 𝐘 ^ w } w = 1 W \{\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{w}\}_{w=1}^{W} . The training loss follows the heatmap-based forecasting formulation in the backbone work. Fig. 4 details the encoder and prediction branches. Lane attention encodes the map into 𝐇 M \mathbf{H}_{\rm M} , a multilayer perceptron embeds spatial coordinates as 𝐇 C \mathbf{H}_{\rm C} , and a trajectory subnet extracts target-vehicle and surrounding-agent features, 𝐇 TV \mathbf{H}_{\rm TV} and 𝐇 S \mathbf{H}_{\rm S} . The interaction module fuses vehicle and map features, which the decoder combines with coordinate features to predict an endpoint heatmap. The regularisation network applies two cross-attention blocks to map, target-vehicle, and coordinate features during training and is removed at inference [ 20 ] . All compared algorithms use this predictor, and evaluation concerns the predicted endpoints. Fig. 4: UQnet backbone (adapted from [ 20 ] ): (a) encoder, (b) regularisation network, used during training and removed at inference, and (c) predictor, which decodes fused map and vehicle features with position features into an endpoint heatmap.

sections.heading: V-B Algorithms and Experimental Coverage
sections.text: We compare four algorithms under the common prediction architecture (Table I ). Vanilla optimises the current task without memory and provides the reference for unconstrained adaptation. DER (dark experience replay) [ 14 ] rehearses stored inputs with output matching to preserve previous predictions, in a forecasting adaptation of the original classification method. SyReM (synergetic memory rehearsal) [ 4 ] combines gradient-based rehearsal selection with an average-memory loss constraint. GSM [ 3 ] is the equal-allocation variant of dynamic gradient scenario memory (D-GSM), with scenario-organised memory (a scenario is one of the four tasks here) and gradient constraints derived from previous scenarios. The selection spans output distillation, selective constrained rehearsal, and scenario-wise constraints, and all memory-based algorithms use a capacity of 2,000 records. sections.heading: VII-A Interpreting the Influence of Task Order
sections.text: Across the 24 orders, task order matters chiefly through the learning quality of the first task. Starting-task identity explains 90% to 99% of the order term in each primary metric, so the across-order component of ( 6 ) is essentially a starting-task component, driven by the cold start of the smallest task. Beyond the first stage, the order effect becomes comparable to training variability and is organised by where task A is placed: the smallest task stays harder to learn at later positions, and its position accounts for half to two-thirds of the residual order term. Within the first stage, DER and SyReM already reach lower cold-start errors than Vanilla and GSM. The transition-direction descriptor inherits this structure. Because the pair containing task A is the more distant pair in every partition of the task set, D D tracks the position of task A, and that position correlates more strongly with every primary metric than D D does. The metric decomposition explains why the same first stage moves CT and BWT in opposite directions: the cold-start error enters CT with weight 1 / N 1/N , whereas in the reference term of BWT = P − B \mathrm{BWT}=P-B the first task carries coefficient 11 / 18 11/18 for N = 4 N=4 . For A-first orders the reference term is an order of magnitude larger than the subsequent error, so the strongly negative BWT records recovery from a poor start, and the order dependence of BWT is largely a reference-term effect.

sections.heading: VII-B Implications for Algorithm Comparison and Benchmark Design
sections.text: Four reporting items follow for continual learning benchmarks. 1. State the order distribution behind every aggregate score, the policy q q in ( 4 ). 2. Report order-resolved and starting-task-resolved outcomes, since changing the order can move a score by far more than changing the algorithm (Tables III and V ). 3. Report the warm-start error CT 2 : N \mathrm{CT}_{2:N} and the final error alongside CT and BWT. 4. Fix any descriptor and weighting rule before the outcomes are seen, so that the policy expresses an intended emphasis. Here, the descriptor-weighted policy took its weighting directions from the present outcomes, put most of its CT weight on orders with task A in the first two positions, and left the ranking unchanged (Table IX ). For the compared algorithms, the clearest result is that SyReM attains the smallest final error and the smallest MR-BWT with bootstrap probability 1.00, leads MR-CT with probability 0.94, and leads all four metrics once the A-first orders are set aside. Final error also separates per-order leaders far more often than CT and BWT (16 or 17 of 24 orders against 2 to 11), and every separable final-error leader is SyReM, so final error is the comparison these replicates resolve most clearly. The interaction term exceeds its within-cell noise level for FDE-CT and FDE-BWT, indicating that algorithms differ in their sensitivity to order. For example, the FDE-CT range across orders is 5.8 m for DER and 6.3 m for SyReM, against 8.2 m for GSM and 8.3 m for Vanilla (Table III ).

sections.heading: VII-C Extension to Other Task Sets
sections.text: The protocol applies to any task set, whereas the magnitudes reported here belong to one benchmark with four tasks, one backbone, and three replicates per cell. For larger N N , sampling from a declared order distribution replaces enumeration, and repeated samples separate coverage uncertainty from training variability. Samples should balance starting tasks, which carried most of the order term here, and the warm-start decomposition should accompany CT. Pre-specifying the descriptor and weights turns the descriptor-weighted policy from the exploratory form used here into a confirmatory one. Task representations beyond vehicle speed, such as distances on the inputs or on backbone features, would extend the protocol to domains without an application-specific variable, and independently constructed task sets will show how far the starting-task effect generalises beyond motion forecasting.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusion
sections.text: This study formulates continual learning evaluation as an expectation over a declared distribution of task orders and applies it to motion forecasting across all 24 orders of four tasks, four algorithms, and three replicates. Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and almost all of this effect comes from the identity of the starting task, acting through the cold start of the smallest task. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability, and most rank reversals between orders lie within it. The first task dominates the reference term of backward transfer, so relative improvement and absolute final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error, and the transition-direction descriptor tracks where the smallest task is placed, leaving the ranking unchanged under descriptor weighting. Benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors make such effects visible and their algorithm comparisons interpretable.

Abstract Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90% to 99% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available here . Index Terms: Benchmark testing, continual learning, evaluation protocol, motion forecasting, task order. Fig. 1: Task order and algorithm comparison. (a) Current-task final displacement error (FDE-CT, m), averaged over three replicates, and algorithm ranking for two orders that differ only in their final two tasks. In both orders the leader lies within one pooled replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. (b) A common order policy q ⁡ ( o ) q(o) , uniform or weighted by the transition descriptor D ⁡ ( o ) D(o) , aggregates the order-resolved outcomes of every algorithm into a uniform mean or weighted score, shown with the range across orders. I Introduction Self-driving vehicles plan their motion around forecasts of where surrounding road users will go. A forecaster trained on urban merges meets highway ramps, intersections, and roundabouts as the fleet expands, and must keep learning in an order no designer controls. Continual learning (CL) provides this capability and is moving into safety-relevant applications. Human-guided CL already uses small amounts of driving guidance to improve self-driving performance in dimensions such as social compliance and rare-case handling [ 1 ] , and continual forecasting methods adapt motion predictors across changing traffic scenarios [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Learning a new task can overwrite earlier knowledge [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Replay, regularisation, and gradient constraints counter this forgetting through different retention mechanisms [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] , so their outcomes depend on the learning history fixed by the task order. Yet the algorithm to deploy is chosen from benchmark rankings. If a ranking reverses when the same tasks arrive in another sequence, that choice hinges on an arbitrary benchmark order. Because outcomes depend on the order in which tasks arrive, any aggregate score for a CL algorithm rests on a distribution over task orders. Evaluating continual forecasting under varying data-stream sequences has been recommended [ 15 ] , yet many protocols leave this distribution implicit, repeating one or a few prescribed orders while varying initialisation or within-task sample order [ 14 , 5 ] . Studies of order-dependent forgetting, order-wise performance disparity, ordering principles, and sequence transferability show that task transitions influence retention and transfer [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] , and use this to explain the outcomes of particular orders, quantify the disparity among them, or select favourable ones. How the variation of a metric across all N ! N! orders of N N tasks, several algorithms, and repeated training runs divides between order, algorithm, their interaction, and training randomness, and which property of an order carries the order effect, remain open. This paper answers both questions for a fixed task set and tests whether algorithm rankings persist across orders. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over an explicit order policy, with the uniform policy as the equal-order reference, and decompose the sum of squares of each metric into order, algorithm, interaction, and training components, splitting the order term by starting task. A replicate bootstrap attaches a probability to every leading algorithm. A warm-start current-task error and a decomposition of backward transfer into subsequent error and initial reference isolate the first learning stage. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics defines a descriptor-weighted policy, an example of a nonuniform policy shared by all algorithms (Figs. 1 (b) and 2 ). The experiments use the UQnet endpoint-heatmap backbone [ 20 ] and four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset: Urban Merge (A), Highway Merge (B), Intersection (C), and Roundabout (D). Vanilla sequential fine-tuning and three memory-based algorithms learn the tasks in all 4 ! = 24 4!=24 orders, with three training replicates per order and algorithm (288 runs). The memory-based algorithms are dark experience replay (DER), synergetic memory rehearsal (SyReM), and gradient scenario memory (GSM). In Fig. 1 (a), A → \to B → \to C → \to D and A → \to B → \to D → \to C differ only in their final two tasks, yet give exactly reversed rankings of the four algorithms by current-task final displacement error. Section VI-A traces both rankings to run-to-run variation in the cold-start error, which arises on the shared first task before the two orders diverge. The main contributions are summarised as follows. 1. Formulation and benchmark. An expectation over an explicit order policy defines a common comparison target, and the law of total variance separates within-order training variation from across-order variation. All 24 orders are enumerated with released per-run results, and the decomposition, adjustment, and bootstrap procedures form a reusable analysis toolkit. 2. Empirical finding. Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90% to 99% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task, acting through the cold start of the smallest task. Beyond the first stage, the residual order effect is comparable to training variability. The per-order leader’s gap to the runner-up exceeds the pooled replicate standard deviation in only 2 to 11 of the 24 orders for current-task error and backward transfer, against 16 or 17 for final error. 3. Metric diagnosis. The first task enters the reference term of stage-averaged backward transfer with weight 11 / 18 11/18 for four tasks, so a poor first fit simultaneously raises current-task error and drives backward transfer towards large negative values. Relative improvement and absolute final error therefore identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. The transition-direction descriptor tracks the position of the smallest task, and the descriptor-weighted policy leaves the full ranking unchanged. Fig. 2: Order-aware evaluation workflow. II Related Work II-A Task Order and Curriculum Effects Curriculum learning investigates the effect of example or task presentation on optimisation [ 21 ] . In CL, ordering also affects retention of previous knowledge. Bell and Lawrence [ 16 ] examine order-dependent forgetting and task-distance heuristics, and Li and Hiratani [ 18 ] derive ordering principles in a teacher–student model. Analyses of task similarity and overparameterisation further characterise interference [ 22 ] . Nguyen et al. [ 23 ] relate error rates to the total complexity of a task sequence and to its sequential heterogeneity, the sum of distances between consecutive tasks. The path length L L in Section IV-D is such a sum. Yoon et al. [ 17 ] quantify order-wise performance disparity, establishing order fairness as an evaluation criterion. Measures of sequence transferability relate task transitions to performance using learned predictors [ 19 ] . The present analysis uses marginal task statistics to define a shared order policy and asks how much of an observed ranking survives a change of order. II-B Continual Learning for Motion Forecasting Continual forecasting addresses adaptation across changing traffic environments [ 15 ] through generative replay [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] , regularisation under distribution shift [ 27 ] , and task-free streams without supplied task boundaries [ 2 , 5 , 28 ] . D-GSM uses traffic divergence and scenario-organised memory to constrain gradient updates [ 3 ] , H2C combines diversity-based selection with equiprobable replay [ 5 ] , SyReM integrates a memory-loss constraint with gradient-based rehearsal selection [ 4 ] , and Dual-LS coordinates long- and short-term knowledge through complementary rehearsal [ 6 ] . These studies evaluate each method along one or a few task orders, so the dependence of the resulting ranking on the order is still unexamined. II-C Evaluation Protocols for Continual Learning Average performance over all tasks, current-task performance, and backward transfer are the standard quantities of continual learning evaluation [ 12 , 29 ] , and the appropriate protocol differs between task-, domain-, and class-incremental settings [ 30 ] . Early protocol studies showed that reported forgetting depends on the evaluation design, including the task sequences used [ 31 , 32 ] , and proposed metric sets beyond final accuracy [ 33 ] . Hyperparameter selection on the evaluation scenario can bias comparisons [ 34 ] , and unequal update costs can alter conclusions about online CL [ 35 ] . Recent benchmarks treat the order either as an adversarial choice to be searched [ 36 ] or as a sampled factor whose uncertainty is reported [ 37 ] . Order coverage is therefore a protocol choice. We distinguish repeated training within an order from evaluation across orders, separate the starting task from the remaining order, and assess backward transfer alongside initial, warm-start, and final error. V-B Algorithms and Experimental Coverage We compare four algorithms under the common prediction architecture (Table I ). Vanilla optimises the current task without memory and provides the reference for unconstrained adaptation. DER (dark experience replay) [ 14 ] rehearses stored inputs with output matching to preserve previous predictions, in a forecasting adaptation of the original classification method. SyReM (synergetic memory rehearsal) [ 4 ] combines gradient-based rehearsal selection with an average-memory loss constraint. GSM [ 3 ] is the equal-allocation variant of dynamic gradient scenario memory (D-GSM), with scenario-organised memory (a scenario is one of the four tasks here) and gradient constraints derived from previous scenarios. The selection spans output distillation, selective constrained rehearsal, and scenario-wise constraints, and all memory-based algorithms use a capacity of 2,000 records.
